chapter: On the road, James Brown and the 1956 crash
title: The night his wife Elizabeth died of a hemorrhage
summary: Cobb relates the evening of February 1970: toast, a cough, bleeding, her death, and telling his daughter.

story.theme_name: Illness, injury and the deaths of colleagues
story.community_name: Illness, injury and death among jazz musicians

blocks.x: Nurse across the street, Marie -- she's a German girl and her husband worked at Borden and all, Borden Milk Company, and normally Rogers is a critical guy, but he sat over here this night, and Marie was teaching my wife how to crochet with needles and things, whatever, and we're looking at a movie, Roger and I together, and finally they sat and sat

and sat until about quarter to 11:00, and Roger said, "I'm hungry." Oh, Elizabeth said, "Oh, man, you can eat anytime." "No," he said, "I'm staying over here since 7:00 something." He said, "I'm hungry now." So they left and went home.

So she come to me, and she said, "You hungry?" I said not really. She said, "How would you like a piece of buttered toast?" I said, "That sounds good." She went and made the buttered toast, and I'm still looking at the movie. She said, "Did you find out who did it yet?" You know, whatever the crime was. I said, "Not yet."

She come in with me, and we sat down and we ate our toast together. We had twin chairs with a table (inaudible). She said, "I feel -- Hoss, I feel like I want another piece. You want another piece?" I said no. She went to fix her another piece of toast. As she stood, asked me, being away from the television, catching me -- find out who it was? I said, "No, not yet."

And she come back in and was looking -- and all of a sudden she gave a cough. She had a white rug in the living room, and it had a plastic runner, and she coughed and a spot of blood about the size of a quarter, and she said, huh-uh-uh. I looked at her, and she wheeled and went in the bathroom. And I got up (inaudible). When I got in the bathroom, just like she turned the faucet on. Blood was everywhere. She hemorrhaged.
Well, how long after the accident was this?
How long after the accident was this?
Well, the accident was in '56. She died in '70.
You mean that's when she died?
I mean she died like this, with the hemorrhage?

Oh, she died -- she was dead before she left the house, but they didn't let me know. And they rushed her out of there and put her in the car. I'd gone in the garage and opened the tailgate to my station wagon for to lay her down in it. I finally got Marie to come over, and Marie's a nurse, so I could get to the doctor. And the doctor said, 'Meet me at the hospital.' And Marie talked to her.
And this was a result of that accident?
Oh, yeah, had to be. It was acute pulmonary hemorrhage. And it comes from weakness of the lungs.
Had -- had she felt all right?
She was feeling good all day, but just one

of those things that happens, and I called Laverne back in Kansas City, and had to tell them that Elizabeth was dead. And Joe was coming to a double funeral. Laverne said, "Don't to Elizabeth today, kid with me. I talked a little, and hung up on me. Then she called me back in an hour, about an hour later. I had called my mother and everything.

My daughter went into a tangent. She was in the room studying for a test the next day. She didn't know what happened. She don't know when they took her mother out. All she knew, she come out and went in the bathroom and saw all this blood, said, "What happened?" I said, Mommy had a hemorrhage." She said, "Will Mommy be all right?" I said, "God knows I hope so."

And we had finished talking about five minutes. Dr. Jones called me. She said, "Arnett?" I said, "Yes, Dr. Jones." And the phone went dead. I knew it had happened. She waited for a while. She said, Elizabeth is dead." I couldn't say nothing.
